Minimal submanifold (H=0)

Words: 38
Riemannian geometry OurBigBook.com
A minimal submanifold has vanishing mean curvature vector, equivalently zero first variation of volume for compactly supported normal variations. A minimal surface is its two-dimensional case. A calibrated submanifold satisfies the stronger property of minimizing volume in its relative homology class.
// Target: general-relativity.bigb

Ricci soliton (Ric+21​LX​g=λg)

Words: 57 Articles: 1
Riemannian geometry OurBigBook.com
A Riemannian metric satisfying the displayed equation for a vector field X and constant λ. A gradient Ricci soliton has X=∇f; it is steady when λ=0.

Steady gradient Ricci soliton scalar identity (R+∣∇f∣2=constant)

Words: 31
Ricci soliton OurBigBook.com
For Ric+∇2f=0, the contracted Bianchi identity and the commutation identity Δ∇f=∇Δf+Ric(∇f) imply ∇R=2Ric(∇f). Meanwhile ∇∣∇f∣2=−2Ric(∇f), so their sum is constant on every connected component.

Riemannian Hessian (Hessg​f=∇df)

Words: 29
Riemannian geometry OurBigBook.com
The symmetric covariant two-tensor defined using the Levi-Civita connection by Hessg​f(X,Y)=X(Yf)−(∇X​Y)f. Its negative metric trace is the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to f. Along a geodesic it gives the second derivative of f.

Spectral geometry

Words: 3k Articles: 36
Riemannian geometry OurBigBook.com
Spectral geometry studies which properties of a Riemannian manifold can be recovered from the spectrum of geometric differential operators, especially the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Explicit spherical harmonics, Fourier series on a flat torus, and isospectral manifolds illustrate three different aspects of the problem.

Wave trace (W(t)=Tr(eitP​))

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Spectral geometry OurBigBook.com
For the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator P on a closed manifold, the wave trace is the distribution ∑j​eitλj​​, counting multiplicities. The series is interpreted after testing against smooth compactly supported functions, rather than as an ordinarily convergent sum. Its singularities relate the spectrum to the length spectrum of closed geodesics, through the Duistermaat-Guillemin trace formula.

Duistermaat-Guillemin trace formula

Words: 75
Wave trace OurBigBook.com
For the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator on a closed manifold, the singular support of the wave trace lies in zero together with signed lengths of closed geodesics. Under the clean fixed-set hypotheses, its singularity at a periodic-geodesic length has an expansion determined by the geodesic flow and its linearized return map. In particular, when the relevant leading coefficient does not vanish through cancellation, that length is determined by the spectrum. The inclusion of singular supports alone does not justify an unconditional recovery of every geodesic length.

Weyl law (N(λ)∼ωd​Vol(M)(2π)−dλd/2)

Words: 53
Spectral geometry OurBigBook.com
For the positive scalar Laplace-Beltrami operator on a closed d-dimensional Riemannian manifold, the number of eigenvalues at most λ, counted with multiplicity, has the displayed leading asymptotic. The exponent determines the dimension and the coefficient determines the total volume of the Riemannian metric. There is an analogous result with fixed Dirichlet boundary conditions or Neumann boundary conditions on a compact smooth domain.

Spectral zeta function (ζL​(s)=∑λj​>0​λj−s​)

Words: 138 Articles: 1
Spectral geometry OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative elliptic operator L on a closed manifold, sum its positive eigenvalues with multiplicity. The defining series converges in a right half-plane. If n0​=dimkerL and K(t)=Tr(e−tL) is the heat trace, then
ζL​(s)=Γ(s)1​∫0∞​ts−1(K(t)−n0​)dt.
(1)
Subtracting finitely many terms of the short-time heat kernel expansion gives a meromorphic continuation. Zero eigenvalues must be excluded: assigning them a nonexistent inverse power does not define the spectral zeta function.

Zero-mode correction to the spectral zeta value (ζL​(0)=at0​−dimkerL)

Words: 77
Spectral zeta function OurBigBook.com
For a Laplace-type operator on a closed manifold, let at0​ be the constant coefficient of its full heat trace expansion. In the Mellin transform defining the spectral zeta function, the reduced trace has constant coefficient at0​−dimkerL. Its contribution is (at0​−dimkerL)/s, and 1/Γ(s)=s+O(s2) proves the identity. For the scalar positive Laplace-Beltrami operator on a closed surface, at0​=∫RdV/(24π) and dimkerL is the number of connected components. In particular, a connected sphere has value −2/3 and a connected flat torus has value −1.

Heat trace (ZM​(t)=Tr(e−tΔM​))

Words: 125 Articles: 1
Spectral geometry OurBigBook.com
For the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator on a closed compact Riemannian manifold, the heat trace is ZM​(t)=∑j​e−tλj​=∫M​KM​(t,x,x)dV(x). It records every eigenvalue with multiplicity. In a finite free isometric quotient it equals ∣U∣−1∑u∈U​∫N​KN​(t,x,ux)dV(x). The orbital integrals form a class function of the ambient finite isometry group, so Gassmann equivalence gives equal quotient heat traces and hence Sunada theorem.

Euler characteristic from the heat trace of a bordered surface ([t0]Tr(e−tP)=χ(M)/6)

Words: 78
Heat trace OurBigBook.com
For a compact smooth Riemannian surface with smooth boundary and a pure Dirichlet boundary condition or pure Neumann boundary condition, the constant coefficient in the heat trace is
12π1​(∫M​KdA+∫∂M​κds)=6χ(M)​.
(2)
The equality is the Gauss-Bonnet theorem. Thus such isospectral manifolds have the same Euler characteristic. A simply connected compact connected bordered surface is a disk with χ=1, whereas a nonorientable surface with c≥1 crosscaps and b≥1 boundary components has χ=2−c−b≤0. These cannot be isospectral in this setting. Corners and mixed boundary conditions contribute additional heat coefficients, so the smooth pure-boundary-condition hypothesis is essential.

Spectrum of the Laplacian on a sphere (λℓ​=ℓ(ℓ+d−1))

Words: 84 Articles: 1
Spectral geometry OurBigBook.com
For the unit Sd and the nonnegative Laplace-Beltrami operator, the eigenvalues are ℓ(ℓ+d−1), with multiplicities (dℓ+d​)−(dℓ+d−2​) for ℓ≥0. The eigenfunctions are restrictions of degree-ℓ harmonic polynomials. The harmonic decomposition of homogeneous polynomials and the Stone-Weierstrass theorem prove completeness.

Ambient restriction formula for the spherical Laplacian (ΔSd​(F∣Sd​)=ΔF−Frr​−dFr​)

Words: 54
Spectrum of the Laplacian on a sphere OurBigBook.com
For a smooth ambient function near the unit sphere, the chain rule along the great circles γi​(t)=pcost+ei​sint gives (F∘γi​)′′(0)=D2F(ei​,ei​)−DF(p). Sum over an orthonormal basis of the tangent space and supplement it by the radial vector p. The geodesic trace formula for the Laplace-Beltrami operator then gives the displayed formula, evaluated at radius one. In particular a degree-ℓ harmonic polynomial restricts to a spherical harmonic with positive eigenvalue ℓ(ℓ+d−1).

Isospectral manifolds (Spec(M)=Spec(N))

Words: 3k Articles: 26
Spectral geometry OurBigBook.com
Two Riemannian manifolds are isospectral for a specified differential operator if their eigenvalues, counted with multiplicities and with the same boundary conditions, agree. Riemannian isometries preserve the Laplace-Beltrami operator spectrum, but the converse can fail. The transplantation theorem and the Sunada theorem give systematic constructions.

Compact isospectral sets of closed surfaces

Words: 61
Isospectral manifolds OurBigBook.com
For a fixed closed orientable Riemannian surface, the smooth metrics with a specified scalar Laplace-Beltrami operator spectrum form a compact set modulo diffeomorphisms, in the smooth topology. This is a compactness assertion, not uniqueness or finiteness of the number of Riemannian isometry classes. It restricts geometric degeneration within an isospectral set and uses more information than the leading heat invariants alone. The theorem was established in the 1988 compactness paper.

Tetra and Didi

Words: 58
Isospectral manifolds OurBigBook.com
A pair of closed orientable flat three-manifolds with equal scalar Laplace-Beltrami operator spectra but different first Betti numbers, respectively one and zero. Consequently they are not homeomorphic. They cannot be isospectral for the Hodge Laplacian on one-forms, whose zero-eigenvalue multiplicity is the first Betti number. This shows why the spectrum on functions must not be silently replaced by the spectra on all differential forms.

Finiteness of isospectral hyperbolic surfaces

Words: 81
Isospectral manifolds OurBigBook.com
For a fixed closed hyperbolic surface, there are only finitely many isometry classes with its Laplacian spectrum. The Selberg trace formula gives a common discrete length spectrum and common positive hyperbolic systole. Mumford's compactness theorem confines this family to a compact subset of moduli space. If distinct members accumulated, choose nearby markings at an accumulation point and use finite length coordinates for hyperbolic surfaces. Each of these finitely many lengths converges while remaining in one discrete spectrum, so it is eventually constant. The length coordinates then force eventual equality, a contradiction. This finiteness theorem is weaker than the Wolpert generic spectral rigidity theorem.

Sunada theorem

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Isospectral manifolds OurBigBook.com
Suppose a finite group G acts by Riemannian isometries on a compact Riemannian manifold M, and Gassmann equivalent subgroups H1​,H2​ act freely. The quotient manifolds Hi​\M have equal Laplace-Beltrami operator spectra. For an eigenfunction space E, the quotient multiplicity is ∣Hi​∣−1∑h∈Hi​​tr(h∣E), and the equality follows by summing its character of a representation over conjugacy classes. Nonconjugacy inside G alone does not guarantee that the quotients are nonisometric.
Sunada orbital heat-trace formula (ZU\N​(t)=∣U∣−1∑u∈U​It​(u))
Words: 78
Sunada theorem OurBigBook.com
For a finite subgroup U of a group T of Riemannian isometries of a closed manifold N, assume U acts freely and define It​(g)=∫N​HN​(t,x,gx)dV(x). Invariance of the Riemannian heat kernel and change of variables show that It​ is a class function on T. For U≤T, the heat kernel on a finite isometric quotient and integration over a fundamental domain give the displayed heat trace formula. Grouping by conjugacy classes proves equality for Gassmann equivalent subgroups. More generally the same argument allows fixed points of T outside the freely acting subgroups; only the quotient under consideration must be smooth.
Sunada unitary equivalence without a finite heat trace (L2(N)Ui​=⨁ρ​VρUi​​⊗Hρ​)
Words: 71
Sunada theorem OurBigBook.com
A finite isometry group decomposes L2(N) into its irreducible representation factors Vρ​ and multiplicity Hilbert spaces Hρ​. The Laplacian commutes with the group, so it acts as the identity on each representation factor. The averaging projection gives dimVρUi​​=∣Ui​∣−1∑u∈Ui​​χρ​(u). For Gassmann equivalent subgroups these dimensions agree. Choosing unitary identifications of the invariant finite-dimensional factors therefore intertwines the quotient Laplacians, even when a noncompact covering manifold has no finite heat trace.
Intersection test for nonisometric finite covers
Words: 273 Articles: 2
Sunada theorem OurBigBook.com
Let two finite locally isometric covers carry uniquely length-identified primitive closed geodesics αi​,βi​. If their geometric intersection numbers differ, the covering surfaces are not isometric, because an isometry preserves both lengths and intersections. For base simple curves intersecting once, lift components correspond to cycles of their monodromy permutations. Their intersection number is the number of sheets common to the two cycles. This distinguishes covers even when every individual permutation has the same cycle type in both actions, as in Gassmann equivalence.
Generic isolation of lifted simple geodesics (ℓ(γ​)=rℓ(γ))
Words: 136
Intersection test for nonisometric finite covers OurBigBook.com
In a finite hyperbolic covering, primitive lifts of a primitive closed geodesic correspond to cycles of its monodromy permutation; an r-cycle gives length rℓ(γ). In a real-analytic family of compact hyperbolic surfaces or hyperbolic cone orbifolds, a prescribed multiple of a simple curve's length can be isolated generically from unrelated lifted lengths. To exclude an identity of length functions, pinch the simple curve: only its peripheral powers can have length tending to zero, while intersecting curves are long by the collar lemma. The countably many remaining length equalities have empty interior, so the Baire category theorem supplies a parameter avoiding them. Only finitely many closed geodesics lie below a fixed local length bound; thus the isolation persists in an open parameter neighbourhood. This makes cycle-intersection information an intrinsic obstruction to an isometry, rather than an invariant of a chosen covering map alone.
Cycle intersections count intersections of lifted curves (i(αC​,β​D​)=∣C∩D∣)
Words: 59
Intersection test for nonisometric finite covers OurBigBook.com
If two simple base geodesics meet once, their lift components correspond to the cycles C,D of their monodromy permutations. A lifted crossing belongs to the sheet labels common to both cycles, giving the displayed geometric intersection count. When their relevant lifted lengths identify these components independently of the covering map, different multisets of intersection counts obstruct an isometry between the covering surfaces.
Cone-torus construction of genus-four Sunada surfaces (7(1−1/7)=6=2g−2)
Words: 179 Articles: 1
Sunada theorem OurBigBook.com
Take a hyperbolic torus with a single cone point of angle 2π/7. Its orbifold fundamental group is ⟨a,d∣[d,a]7=1⟩. An epimorphism to PSL(3,2) whose commutator has exact order 7 has torsion-free kernel. The point and line stabilizers have index 7 and order 24, hence avoid all nontrivial cone stabilizers. Their quotient covers are smooth surfaces with Euler characteristic 7(−6/7)=−6, so have genus 4. Their equal coset permutation characters give equal heat traces by the Sunada theorem. Nonisometry still requires a geometric distinction, such as the intersection test for nonisometric finite covers.
Lambert quadrilateral construction of a cone torus (sinhxsinhy=cos(π/14))
Words: 99
Cone-torus construction of genus-four Sunada surfaces OurBigBook.com
A Lambert quadrilateral with acute angle π/14 and sides x,y incident to the opposite right-angle vertex satisfies the displayed relation. Reflect four copies around that vertex to make a symmetric hyperbolic quadrilateral whose four corner angles are π/14. Identifying opposite sides yields a torus with one cone angle 2π/7. The two central axis loops have lengths 2x,2y and meet once at right angles. Cutting along one loop gives a pair of pants with two equal geodesic boundaries and the cone point; reglue the boundaries with a Fenchel–Nielsen twist to obtain the two-parameter cone-torus family. Its seven-sheeted torsion-free covers have genus four.
Triangle cover construction for Sunada surfaces (χ(M)=∣T∣(p−1+q−1+r−1−1))
Words: 125 Articles: 1
Sunada theorem OurBigBook.com
Let a finite group T be generated by elements of exact orders p,q whose product has exact order r, with p−1+q−1+r−1<1. The epimorphism from the hyperbolic triangle group sending its generators to these elements has torsion-free kernel. Its quotient of the hyperbolic plane is a closed surface with a T action. A subgroup acts freely precisely when it meets no conjugate of a nonidentity power of the three elliptic generators. Free almost conjugate subgroups give isospectral manifolds by the Sunada theorem.
Reflection intertwining of triangle-cover coset actions (RAU​R−1=AV−1​,RBU​R−1=BV−1​)
Words: 54
Triangle cover construction for Sunada surfaces OurBigBook.com
Write triangle-group generators as products a=s1​s2​, b=s2​s3​ of adjacent side reflections. Conjugation by s2​ sends both to their inverses. A sheet relabelling satisfying the displayed two permutation identities therefore lifts this base reflection to an orientation-reversing isometry between the two hyperbolic covers. Thus nonconjugate subgroups in the orientation-preserving finite group can still give isometric covers.
Curvature markers distinguishing finite-cover quotients
Words: 183
Sunada theorem OurBigBook.com
For a finite isometric group action on a closed Riemannian surface, choose a disk in the free locus whose translates are disjoint. Modify the Riemannian metric there, and identically on its translates, by small supported changes with three distinguished high Gaussian curvature maxima. Give their heights distinct values occurring nowhere else, arrange them as a tight noncollinear cluster, and keep separate clusters far apart. Such markers can be made by local conformal bump functions controlling curvature and its derivatives. Every quotient isometry must send an entire labelled cluster to another. After identifying the marked disks with the original one, an isometry fixes its three noncollinear points and is therefore the identity locally. If pi​:M→Ui​\M are free finite quotients, any quotient isometry F consequently makes F∘p1​=p2​∘t on an open disk for some element t of the original group. Two local isometries agreeing on an open set agree on the connected surface, by propagation along geodesics. The equality therefore holds globally and implies tU1​t−1⊆U2​, hence equality for equal subgroup orders. Nonconjugate equal-order subgroups thus have nonisometric quotients for this marked invariant metric; constant curvature is not required.
Area separation of convergent Sunada families (area(hk​)=area(h0​)(1+2−k))
Words: 129
Sunada theorem OurBigBook.com
Suppose a fixed pair of Gassmann equivalent finite covers of a compact two-dimensional orbifold has isometric limiting hyperbolic metrics. Choose nearby orbifold-smooth nowhere locally homogeneous metrics and rescale them to the displayed distinct areas. Scaling by a positive constant multiplies area by that constant in dimension two, preserves local rigidity, and preserves convergence when the constants tend to one. Sunada theorem supplies equal spectra within each pair. Local rigidity forces any quotient isometry to descend to the identity on the base; nonconjugate covering subgroups therefore exclude within-pair isometry. Distinct areas exclude all cross-pair isometries and spectra, because the leading heat trace coefficient is area divided by 4πt. Fixed markings of the two isometric limiting covers give convergence to the same metric. The existence of those isometric limits is an additional geometric input, not a consequence of Gassmann equivalence alone.

A class of metrics is spectrally rigid if equality of their specified spectra forces the metrics to be isometric, or, in a deformation version, if continuous isospectral deformations are trivial. Spectral rigidity OurBigBook.com
For closed hyperbolic surfaces of genus g≥2, there is a closed proper real-analytic exceptional subset of Teichmüller space such that a surface outside it is determined up to isometry by its unmarked length spectrum, equivalently its Laplace-Beltrami operator spectrum. The analytic part of the proof controls possible spectral matchings using finite determining length data; the geometric part recognizes persistent matchings as changes of marking, using the collar lemma and variations of Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates. Orientation reversal remains invisible to the spectrum.

Riemannian manifold OurBigBook.com
A linear isometry between tangent spaces of complete simply connected Riemannian manifolds extends to a global isometry when parallel transport along corresponding broken geodesics identifies their Riemann curvature tensors. In particular, complete simply connected manifolds of the same dimension and constant sectional curvature are isometric: their curvature tensors are determined by that common constant and their Riemannian metrics. This is the constant-curvature form often called Cartan's theorem.

Riemannian manifold OurBigBook.com
For a connected complete Riemannian manifold of dimension n≥2 and constant sectional curvature k>0, its complete simply connected universal cover is the round sphere of radius k−1/2. This is the constant-curvature case of Cartan-Ambrose-Hicks theorem. Thus the manifold is a quotient by a finite group of isometries acting freely. In even dimension, the determinant embeds this group in {1,−1}: every determinant-one orthogonal transformation in odd ambient dimension has eigenvalue one and therefore a fixed point. The only possible nonidentity element is the antipodal involution, giving Real projective space. In odd dimensions, free cyclic scalar actions on complex unit spheres instead produce lens spaces.

The condition is local and does not assert that global point reflections extend to isometries of the whole manifold.

Riemannian manifold OurBigBook.com
A Riemannian manifold is homogeneous when its isometry group acts transitively on points. For example, a Lie group with a left-invariant metric is homogeneous under left translations. Two-point homogeneous Riemannian manifold OurBigBook.com

One direction follows by taking short equal-length radial geodesic segments: the Gauss lemma identifies their distance, and injectivity of the exponential map identifies the initial directions after the endpoints are matched. Conversely, unit tangent transitivity implies point homogeneity, hence completeness. The Hopf-Rinow theorem supplies minimizing geodesics for arbitrary equal-distance pairs. Matching their initial unit tangent vectors and using uniqueness of the geodesic equation matches their other endpoints.

A geodesic γ:I→M is maximal when it has no geodesic extension to a strictly larger interval. Every initial position and velocity determine a unique maximal geodesic through the geodesic equation.

An extendible geodesic is a geodesic segment that can be continued beyond at least one endpoint within the same manifold after retaining an affine parameter. An artificial truncation at a regular event is extendible even when its continuation eventually reaches a singularity.

Geodesic completeness

Complete geodesic OurBigBook.com
A Riemannian manifold is geodesically complete when every maximal geodesic is defined for every real affine parameter, equivalently when every exponential map is defined on its entire tangent space.
Upward stability of Riemannian completeness (g​≥g,g complete⟹g​ complete)
Words: 57
Geodesic completeness OurBigBook.com
Pointwise domination of Riemannian metrics gives domination of their distances. A Cauchy sequence for the larger distance is Cauchy for the complete smaller one. Smooth positive metrics induce the same manifold topology, so its limit is also a limit in the larger distance. The Hopf-Rinow theorem turns metric completeness into geodesic completeness. Mere positivity of the second metric, without domination, is insufficient.
Compact-core completeness for a Euclidean end (KR​=X∪Φ−1{1<∣x∣≤R} compact)
Words: 79
Geodesic completeness OurBigBook.com
Suppose these sets exhaust a manifold, and its Riemannian metric is Euclidean beyond some radius in the end coordinates. A finite-time geodesic has fixed speed and cannot increase its exterior radius faster than that speed. It remains in one compact core enlargement, with velocity in a compact disk bundle. The geodesic equation therefore continues beyond every finite parameter endpoint. The compactness hypothesis is substantive: the open exterior of a closed Euclidean ball, with empty core, is incomplete at its inner boundary despite having a Euclidean metric at infinity.

Hopf-Rinow theorem
Words: 235 Articles: 2
Geodesic completeness OurBigBook.com
For a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, completeness of the Riemannian distance, geodesic completeness, and compactness of every closed bounded subset are equivalent. These conditions imply that any two points are joined by a minimizing geodesic. Pairwise existence of minimizing geodesics alone does not imply completeness: an open Euclidean ball is incomplete, yet the line segment between any two of its points stays in the ball and minimizes length.
Hopf-Rinow lemma
Words: 79
Hopf-Rinow theorem OurBigBook.com
If the Riemannian exponential map at one point p of a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold is defined on all of Tp​M, every point can be joined to p by a minimizing geodesic. The distance splitting through a small geodesic sphere selects a radial direction attaining d(p,q)=r+d(γ(r),q). If this equality stopped before the target, repeat the splitting at its last point. A broken minimizing path cannot have a corner, so the new segment continues the same geodesic, contradicting maximality. This is the minimizing-geodesic lemma used in the radial continuation proof of Hopf-Rinow.
// Target: riemannian-geometry.bigb
Radial continuation proof of Hopf-Rinow
Words: 99
Hopf-Rinow theorem OurBigBook.com
Assume geodesic completeness. Minimize the distance to a target over a small compact geodesic sphere about the initial point. The distance splitting through a small geodesic sphere gives an initial direction satisfying d(p,γ(t))+d(γ(t),q)=d(p,q). If this equality stops before the target, repeat the splitting at the last equality point. The resulting broken path minimizes, so its corner must smooth into the same continuing geodesic, a contradiction. This supplies a minimizing geodesic to every target. Every closed metric ball is then the image under the Riemannian exponential map of a closed tangent ball, hence compact. A Cauchy sequence has a convergent subsequence in such a ball and therefore converges, proving metric completeness without presupposing a global minimizing curve.

Line in a Riemannian manifold

Words: 161 Articles: 2
Geodesic OurBigBook.com
A line is a unit-speed geodesic γ:R→M that minimizes between every two of its points: dg​(γ(s),γ(t))=∣s−t∣.
This is a globally minimizing geodesic, a Riemannian specialization of the general geometric line notion.

Disconnected at infinity

Words: 128 Articles: 1
Line in a Riemannian manifold OurBigBook.com
A connected noncompact manifold is disconnected at infinity when the complement of some compact subset has at least two unbounded connected components. Equivalently, it has at least two ends.
The relevant general concept is an End; having several ends is a property of the space, not a synonym for one end.
A line from disconnection at infinity
Words: 77
Disconnected at infinity OurBigBook.com
A connected complete Riemannian manifold that is disconnected at infinity contains a line in a Riemannian manifold. Choose points escaping in two components outside a fixed compact set and join them by minimizing geodesics. Each segment crosses the compact set. Parametrize from a crossing point; both parameter endpoints tend to infinity in opposite directions. Compactness of the unit tangent vectors over the crossing set gives a subsequence converging to an entire geodesic. Every finite subsegment is minimizing by continuity of distance, so the limit is a line.

Geodesic OurBigBook.com
If two embedded surfaces are tangent along a curve, their tangent planes agree there. The curve's ambient acceleration is normal to one surface exactly when it is normal to the other, so it is a geodesic of one exactly when it is a geodesic of the other.

A circular helix on a circular cylinder has radial ambient acceleration and is therefore a geodesic. Any surface tangent to the cylinder along that helix has the same curve as a geodesic.

Energy of a curve OurBigBook.com
A fixed-endpoint variation of a curve γ:[a,b]→S is a smooth family Γ(s,t) with Γ(0,t)=γ(t), Γ(s,a)=γ(a) and Γ(s,b)=γ(b). Its variation vector field V(t)=∂s​Γ(0,t) vanishes at the endpoints. Consequently integration by parts in the first variation of energy of a curve has no boundary contribution, and stationarity is characterized by the geodesic equation.

Jacobi fields form the radical of the fixed-endpoint index form
Words: 71
Riemannian index form OurBigBook.com
On continuous piecewise smooth vector field along a curve with zero endpoints, the radical of a bilinear form of the Riemannian index form is exactly the space of endpoint-vanishing Jacobi fields. Integration by parts against tests supported inside each smooth piece gives the Jacobi equation; tests with arbitrary values at breakpoints force continuity of the covariant derivative, hence a global smooth Jacobi field. This characterization uses I(V,W)=0 for every test field W, not merely I(V,V)=0, which is insufficient for an indefinite form.

Conjugate-point criterion for the Riemannian index form
Words: 146 Articles: 1
Riemannian index form OurBigBook.com
On continuous piecewise smooth perpendicular fields with zero endpoints, the Riemannian index form is nonnegative exactly when no point strictly inside the geodesic segment is conjugate to its initial point. It is positive on every nonzero field exactly when no conjugate point occurs up to and including the final endpoint. At a first conjugate endpoint its nullspace consists of the endpoint-vanishing Jacobi fields. These statements distinguish nonnegative quadratic forms from strictly positive ones and do not assume global minimization.

Words: 74
Conjugate-point criterion for the Riemannian index form OurBigBook.com
Let a nonzero Jacobi field J vanish at times zero and a. On a longer geodesic segment ending at b>a, extend it by zero to a continuous piecewise smooth field Z. Then I(Z,Z)=0. Choose an endpoint-vanishing field P with P(a)=−Dt​J(a); integration by parts gives I(Z,P)=−∣Dt​J(a)∣2<0. Thus I(Z+εP,Z+εP)<0 for small positive ε. Smooth approximation preserves negativity. The second variation of geodesic energy supplies a shorter path, so a minimizing geodesic cannot extend beyond its first conjugate point.

Instability of a closed geodesic in positive even-dimensional curvature
Words: 82
Second variation of geodesic energy OurBigBook.com
On an oriented even-dimensional Riemannian manifold of strictly positive sectional curvature, a nonconstant closed geodesic has a length-decreasing smooth variation. Its parallel transport fixes the tangent and acts on the odd-dimensional normal space by a special orthogonal group element. An odd-dimensional special orthogonal transformation has a fixed vector, so there is a nonzero periodic parallel normal field V. The second variation of geodesic energy is then strictly negative. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality converts lower energy into strictly lower length because the original geodesic has constant speed. For an embedded geodesic the small variation is a smooth isotopy; otherwise it is a deformation through immersed loops.

Unparametrized geodesic equation (∇v​v=fv)

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Geodesic equation OurBigBook.com
A regular curve with tangent v=dx/du is an unparametrized geodesic of an affine connection if ∇v​v=f(u)v. Choose a new parameter s with ds/du=r(u)>0 and r′/r=f. Then w=dx/ds=v/r obeys ∇w​w=r−2(∇v​v−(r′/r)v)=0. Conversely a reparametrized affine geodesic has acceleration proportional to its tangent. This criterion concerns the geometric curve, not a fixed parametrization.

Timelike length and energy have the same geodesic images

Words: 92
Unparametrized geodesic equation OurBigBook.com
For a Lorentzian metric and timelike v=dx/du, put L=−g(v,v)​>0 and L=L2/2. The Euler-Lagrange equations of L give ∇v​v=0, while those of L give ∇v​v=(L˙/L)v. Taking ds/du=L removes the latter tangential acceleration and gives a unit timelike tangent. Thus the two actions have the same geodesic images; the quadratic action singles out an affine parameter. They do not have the same solutions for an arbitrary fixed parameter: t=u2, x=0, u>0, in Minkowski spacetime solves the length equation but not the energy equation. Null curves are excluded since L=0.

On a connected Riemannian manifold of dimension at least three, pointwise independence of sectional curvature from the tangent two-plane forces the curvature to be constant. The contracted Bianchi identity differentiates the relation Ric=(n−1)Kg and gives (n−2)dK=0.

Riemannian geometry OurBigBook.com
A (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold is geodesically complete when every inextendible affinely parametrized geodesic is defined for all real parameter values.
